key_finding: Across six long-horizon search agents on BrowseComp-Plus and BrowseComp, answer accuracy correlates more with cumulative retrieval recall than with number of searches, and the best-performing agents issue far fewer redundant reformulated queries.
methodology: Trajectory-level diagnosis using human-annotated document-level relevance judgments, comparing six agents on BrowseComp-Plus and validating on BrowseComp, with retrieval model and evaluation harness held fixed.
why_it_matters: Directly targets Q2/Q4: search effort (query count, context consumed) is only weakly tied to gains, while retrieval-evidence quality drives accuracy — undercutting the assumption that more agentic searching itself produces the improvement, and pointing to stopping-criteria design instead.
limitations: Evaluated on curated deep-research benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus/BrowseComp) rather than open scientific-literature corpora
only six agents sampled, may not cover the full design space
relevance_reason: Diagnoses which specific agentic behaviors (search volume, reformulation, evidence use) actually carry measured gains, the core mechanism-attribution question.

key_finding: PaSa-7B surpasses the best Google-based baseline by 37.78% in recall@20 and 39.90% in recall@50 on RealScholarQuery, and exceeds a prompted GPT-4o paper-search agent by 30.36% in recall.
methodology: RL-trained LLM agent that searches, reads, and selects references, trained on a synthetic 35k-query AutoScholarQuery set and evaluated on a separately built RealScholarQuery benchmark against Google/Google Scholar/ChatGPT-search baselines.
why_it_matters: Establishes a large, quantified recall gap between agentic scholar search and single-query search-engine baselines (Q1) and models a benchmark-construction split (synthetic train / real-world eval) worth measuring our own evaluation sets against (Q3).
limitations: Synthetic training queries drawn from top-tier AI conference papers, so generalization beyond CS is untested
some baselines are paraphrase-augmented single queries rather than careful human search sessions
relevance_reason: A foundational agentic paper-search system quantifying the baseline-vs-agent recall gap and describing benchmark construction in detail.

key_finding: Crase, a bounded citation-graph exploration agent (single seed query, 1.5-hop citation expansion, entailment-based pruning, recency-aware random-walk ranking), outperforms proprietary-model deep research agents by up to 3x recall@50 at roughly a third of the cost on LitSearch and a second benchmark over a 500K-paper arXiv corpus.
methodology: Bounded graph-traversal pipeline (seed retrieval + citation-graph expansion + entailment-based edge pruning + recency-aware ranking) benchmarked against open-ended deep-research agents on two scholarly search benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Isolates citation-graph traversal as the specific mechanism carrying the gain (Q2), and shows a bounded, inspectable design beats open-ended agentic search loops at lower cost — directly actionable for which agentic move to build.
limitations: Evaluated only on LitSearch and one further arXiv-restricted benchmark, may not generalize beyond CS/physics preprints
comparison against proprietary deep-research agents whose exact configuration is opaque
relevance_reason: Directly attributes a measured recall gain to citation-graph traversal specifically, versus open-ended agentic search as a whole.

key_finding: Across eight parallel human-vs-AI literature-review tasks, overlap between human- and AI-selected references was under 6%, and 64% of mid-2025 AI-generated references contained at least one incorrect metadata field, though a single-project test with a 2026 model showed zero fabrication or mismatch.
methodology: Controlled parallel study: human experts and AI prompters (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT Deep Research, Gemini) independently perform identical literature-review tasks across eight physics/astrophysics/cosmology research projects.
why_it_matters: Directly answers Q4: mid-2025 agentic/LLM literature search does not reproduce expert reference selection (<6% overlap) and carries a high metadata-hallucination rate, undercutting the premise that agentic literature-search gains are already real and reliable.
limitations: Only eight expert-conceived projects, a small sample
domain restricted to physics/astrophysics/cosmology
improvement claimed for the 2026 model is based on a single-project test
relevance_reason: Empirically measures how far current agentic literature search diverges from expert search, directly testing the brief's premise.

key_finding: WisPaper achieves 22.26% recall on TaxoBench versus 20.92% for an O3 baseline, while its validation module WisModel attains 93.70% validation accuracy against retrieval hallucinations.
methodology: End-to-end agent system with Scholar Search (keyword search plus agentic Deep Search validation), Library, and AI Feeds modules, evaluated on TaxoBench recall.
why_it_matters: The reported agentic-vs-baseline recall gain here is small (~1.3 points), which is useful evidence tempering how large a gain undifferentiated end-to-end agentic systems actually deliver over a strong baseline (Q1/Q2).
limitations: TaxoBench's construction is not detailed in the abstract
the specific mechanism driving the small gain (deep-search validation vs keyword search) is not isolated
relevance_reason: Reports a small, quantified agentic-system-vs-baseline recall gain relevant to the recall-ceiling question.

key_finding: ReBOL, which uses LLM query reformulations to seed a Bayesian-optimization posterior over document relevance refined via batched LLM scoring, achieves 46.5% vs 35.0% recall@100 and 63.6% vs 61.2% NDCG@10 versus the best LLM reranker baseline on Robust04, at comparable latency.
methodology: Bayesian optimization over document relevance initialized by LLM query reformulations and iteratively refined by batched LLM relevance scoring, evaluated on five BEIR datasets with two LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-5.2).
why_it_matters: Concretely shows where plain query-reformulation-then-vector-retrieval fails, and quantifies how much of the recall gain comes from iterative relevance re-scoring versus reformulation alone — directly informs the retrieval layer underneath agentic literature-search systems (Q3).
limitations: Evaluated on general BEIR datasets rather than a scientific-literature-search-specific benchmark
cost/latency at larger corpus scales than BEIR is not characterized
relevance_reason: Describes and quantifies a retrieval/reranking technique combining query reformulation with iterative relevance optimization.

key_finding: In a pre-registered two-arm study on a planted wiki-style corpus, removing followable cross-reference links roughly doubled searches-per-grounded-fact as corpus size scaled to 5000 pages, while grounded coverage stayed at ceiling in every condition via read-derived re-search.
methodology: Pre-registered, deterministic, planted-corpus experiment (50/500/5000 pages) contrasting real hyperlinks against meaning-preserving prose, measured via an MCP-exposed search/fetch agent across 99 episodes with fully reproducible offline analysis.
why_it_matters: Its causal-isolation design for measuring how link/graph structure changes agent search cost is a rigorous instrument that could inform how citation-graph-traversal benefits get isolated in literature-search benchmarks, but the corpus is an organizational wiki, not scientific literature.
limitations: Corpus is a synthetic organizational wiki, not a scientific literature corpus
single agent (Claude) tested via a single MCP server
generalization from generic hyperlinks to citation-graph structure specifically is untested
relevance_reason: Rigorously isolates the causal effect of link/graph traversal on agent search cost, a mechanism analogous to citation-graph traversal, but outside the brief's literature-search setting.

key_finding: LATTICE achieves 46.7 nDCG@10 on the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark — matching the best fine-tuned ensemble baseline — while an ensemble variant, LATTICE++, reaches 49.1 nDCG@10, using LLM-guided hierarchical corpus traversal instead of an embedding retriever.
methodology: LLM-guided hierarchical search index built via top-down LLM judgments over multi-level document summaries, with calibrated path-aggregated traversal at query time; evaluated on BRIGHT, NQ, SciFact, and SciDocs.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that standard embedding-based top-k retrieval is a real recall bottleneck for reasoning-intensive queries and that LLM-guided traversal can match fine-tuned ensembles without an embedder in the loop — a concrete alternative retrieval layer for agentic literature-search systems (Q1/Q3).
limitations: BRIGHT is a reasoning-intensive IR benchmark, not itself a literature-search benchmark
index-construction cost and scalability to large scientific corpora are not detailed
relevance_reason: Direct evidence on retrieval/reranking method design and on where embedding-based baselines break down for reasoning-heavy queries.

key_finding: On BrowseComp-Plus's fixed, human-verified corpus, Search-R1 with BM25 achieves only 3.86% accuracy, GPT-5 alone reaches 55.9%, and GPT-5 with a Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever reaches 70.1% while issuing fewer search calls.
methodology: Introduces a fixed-corpus benchmark derived from BrowseComp with human-verified supporting documents and mined hard negatives, enabling controlled, reproducible separation of retriever quality from agent reasoning.
why_it_matters: The central artifact for Q1/Q3: gives a controlled way to disentangle retriever from agent contribution and shows the enormous swing (3.86%→70.1%) retriever choice alone produces, a figure any claimed agentic gain must be measured against.
limitations: Corpus, though fixed, is derived from BrowseComp and inherits any construction biases of the original benchmark
exact corpus size and negative-mining details not given in this abstract
relevance_reason: The field's reference benchmark for isolating retriever effect from agent reasoning, essential to the baseline-ceiling and benchmark-construction questions.

key_finding: Deep research agents exhibit an 'inertia bias' — degraded objectivity when judging the consequences of their own prior actions — and NIS-Agent, which isolates context at webpage-triage and final-answer-validation points, achieves competitive performance on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-zh while cutting token cost by 33%.
methodology: Introduces the IBIS benchmark to control search observations while varying self-authorship of prior actions, then evaluates a context-isolation intervention (NIS-Agent) across four deep-research benchmarks, including an 8B model trained for bias resistance.
why_it_matters: Identifies a specific internal failure mode inside 'the agentic system as a whole' that helps explain variance in reported agentic gains across benchmarks, relevant to Q2's mechanism-attribution and Q4's search for where gains break down.
limitations: IBIS is a new, narrowly-scoped benchmark built around a single bias
reported improvement is a cost reduction with competitive, not superior, accuracy
relevance_reason: Attributes part of agentic system performance/failure to a specific internal mechanism rather than treating the system as undifferentiated.

key_finding: HySemRAG's structured field extraction achieves 35.1% higher semantic similarity (0.655 vs 0.485, p<0.000001) than PDF-chunking approaches, with its agentic QA loop achieving 68.3% single-pass success and 99.0% citation accuracy across 643 observations.
methodology: Eight-stage hybrid RAG pipeline (semantic search, keyword filtering, knowledge-graph traversal, agentic self-correction, citation verification) evaluated across 60 testing sessions and applied to geospatial epidemiology literature.
why_it_matters: A concrete hybrid retrieval architecture (semantic + keyword + graph traversal) for literature synthesis (Q3), though evaluated on an internal, application-specific test set rather than a shared benchmark.
limitations: Evaluation set (643 observations, 60 sessions) is internal and not externally validated
case-study domain (ozone/cardiovascular epidemiology) differs from the CS-methods setting the brief centers on
relevance_reason: Describes a hybrid retrieval/reranking architecture underlying an agentic literature-synthesis system.

key_finding: A systematic taxonomy of Deep Research agent architectures (static vs dynamic workflows, single- vs multi-agent, API- vs browser-based retrieval) paired with a critical evaluation of current benchmarks' limitations, including restricted knowledge access and metric-objective misalignment.
methodology: Narrative systematic review and taxonomy synthesis of Deep Research agent designs and benchmarks. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides the shared vocabulary and benchmark critique the rest of the scan's findings should be organized against, and explicitly flags metric-objective misalignment — exactly the kind of gain-inflation risk Q4 asks us to watch for.
limitations: Narrative review rather than a systematic-review protocol or empirical study
abstract-only, so specific quantitative claims about benchmark flaws are not given
relevance_reason: A comprehensive review synthesizing the agentic deep-research design space and its benchmark critiques.

key_finding: Relocating BrowseComp-Plus's evidence into an independently-built 553M-document corpus (ClimbMix) drops the strongest agent's evidence recall from 84.3% to 21.4% and answer accuracy by five points, while requiring 63% more search calls.
methodology: A projection pipeline decomposes benchmark questions into atomic reasoning hops and re-grounds each hop in a new corpus, validated by automatic verification, an independent agent, and human review; applied to 830 BrowseComp-Plus questions, yielding 57 fully-grounded questions.
why_it_matters: Directly answers Q4 for the field's flagship controlled benchmark: BrowseComp-Plus's per-query-curated corpus inflates evidence recall relative to an independently constructed corpus, meaning reported agentic gains on it likely overstate real-world retrieval difficulty.
limitations: Yields only 57 grounded questions from an original 830, a large reduction in evaluable set size
tested against a single projection target (ClimbMix); generalization to other corpora is untested
relevance_reason: Directly demonstrates a reported agentic-search benchmark result shrinking under an independently constructed corpus — precisely the gain-replication-failure question.

key_finding: PaperPilot's editable-workflow agent raises Hit@5 from 58.0 to 77.0, MRR from 47.5 to 59.4, and nDCG@10 from 26.8 to 32.5 over a base toolset agent, while cutting workflow execution errors from 9.5% to 0%.
methodology: 9B-parameter agent trained via supervised workflow imitation plus preference optimization over corrupted workflows; evaluated in multi-turn interaction against a Qwen3.5-9B toolset baseline.
why_it_matters: Shows the gain from an explicit, DAG-structured search workflow (keyword search, citation expansion, reranking as separate operators) rather than a monolithic agent, directly informing which agentic moves to instrument and measure separately.
limitations: comparison baseline is another agentic system, not a single-query DB search ceiling
benchmark construction for the Hit@5/MRR/nDCG numbers is not described
relevance_reason: A core in-window system paper decomposing agentic literature search into inspectable, separately-scored operators, directly bearing on questions 1-3.

key_finding: EviReform's evidence-guided residual query reformulation improves graph retrieval by up to 5.59 Recall@5 and 4.50 F1 points over the strongest baseline on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
methodology: Separates query revision from evidence aggregation in graph retrieval; normalizes and combines original and residual retrieval signals; evaluated on three standard multi-hop QA benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Cleanly isolates query reformulation as the mechanism carrying a measured gain in graph retrieval, the exact kind of decomposition question 2 asks for, though demonstrated on general multi-hop QA rather than literature search.
limitations: evaluated on multi-hop QA benchmarks, not scientific literature retrieval
no scientific-paper corpus or citation-graph specifics tested
relevance_reason: Directly relevant retrieval/reformulation technique but in a different retrieval setting than the brief's literature-search focus.

key_finding: Of 24 coded runnable AI-scientist systems, 83% release code but only 38% release seeds/traces and 38% report any novelty-verification method, and no closed-loop system demonstrates an externally validated in-loop oracle.
methodology: Systematic screening of 125 candidate works, 35 included, 26 full-text coded across seven audit dimensions (lifecycle stage, autonomy, evaluation, artifacts, human-in-loop, novelty verification, result-selection disclosure).
why_it_matters: Warns that claim-verification and reproducibility artifacts lag code release across the full AI-scientist pipeline, which should temper how much we trust self-reported gains from literature-search sub-systems within these pipelines.
limitations: covers the whole research lifecycle, not literature search benchmarks specifically
abstract gives no numbers on literature-search stage results alone
relevance_reason: A synthesis of verification/reproducibility gaps across agentic research systems, feeding the scan's skepticism about reported gains (Q4) even though its scope is broader than literature search alone.

key_finding: PaSaMaster achieves 16.5x higher F1 than Google Scholar and 37.8% higher F1 than GPT-5.2 at about 1% of the cost, while reducing citation hallucination from 32.66% to zero across 38 disciplines in PaSaMaster-Bench.
methodology: Recursive self-evolving retrieval agent separating frontier-LLM intent understanding from lightweight-model retrieval/scoring over verified papers; evaluated on a custom 38-discipline benchmark against Google Scholar and GPT-5.2.
why_it_matters: Directly anchors the recall/precision gap between plain search-engine baselines (Google Scholar) and an agentic, self-evolving retrieval loop, giving concrete magnitude for question 1 and 2.
limitations: benchmark (PaSaMaster-Bench) construction details (labeling, contamination control) not given in the abstract
comparison baseline is Google Scholar rather than a controlled single-query BM25/embedding search
relevance_reason: Provides a quantified agentic-vs-baseline comparison plus a hallucination-reduction claim central to the brief's core questions.

key_finding: PaperQA2 matches or exceeds subject-matter-expert performance on literature search, summarization, and contradiction-detection tasks, and identifies 2.34+/-1.99 contradictions per paper with 70% expert-validated.
methodology: Human-AI comparison methodology on real-world literature research tasks with unrestricted human access to internet/tools; introduces the LitQA2 benchmark that guided PaperQA2's design.
why_it_matters: The foundational, heavily-cited demonstration that an agentic literature-search system can exceed human experts, and its LitQA2 construction is a direct precedent for how the brief's question-3 benchmarks should be built and scrutinized.
limitations: abstract gives no direct single-query baseline recall figure to anchor comparisons
focuses on biology literature, may not generalize across all scientific domains
relevance_reason: The field's central reference point that later agentic literature-search claims are measured against or argue with.

key_finding: Across Chronos and provider CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI), grep generally outperforms vector retrieval on a 116-question LongMemEval sample, with overall scores strongly dependent on harness and tool-calling style.
methodology: Two empirical experiments comparing grep vs vector retrieval across multiple agent harnesses, with inline vs file-based tool outputs and progressively distracting context.
why_it_matters: Undercuts the assumption that dense/embedding retrieval is the stronger default tool for agentic search loops, suggesting harness and retrieval-style choice matter more than the retrieval paradigm itself — relevant caution for question 1's baseline framing.
limitations: evaluated on conversational memory (LongMemEval), not scientific literature corpora
no scientific-paper citation graph or literature benchmark tested
relevance_reason: A rigorous, contradicting empirical result about retrieval-method choice in agent loops, though in a non-literature-search setting.

key_finding: GraphRAG-Bench shows GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks, and systematically maps the conditions under which graph structure actually helps.
methodology: New benchmark spanning fact retrieval, complex reasoning, contextual summarization, and creative generation, with systematic pipeline evaluation from graph construction through generation.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that citation/knowledge-graph traversal does not reliably beat plain retrieval-augmented generation, which is exactly the failure-to-replicate pattern question 4 asks the scan to surface.
limitations: general RAG tasks rather than scientific literature search specifically
graph type is general knowledge graph, not citation graph over papers
relevance_reason: A benchmark explicitly testing when graph-based retrieval helps or fails, directly informing the brief's skepticism about agentic graph-traversal gains.

key_finding: DynaKRAG's shared state-conditioned policy for coordinating iterative retrieval, reformulation, and sufficiency checking ranks first in EM/F1 across nine dataset-backbone pairs while cutting token use 10.1-34.3% and retrieval calls 15.1-43.4%.
methodology: Learned policy with a deterministic validity layer, continuation gate, and advantage scorer; evaluated on HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and MuSiQue with three LLM backbones.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates measurable efficiency and quality gains from decomposing multi-hop evidence acquisition into distinct learned operations, a template for isolating agentic-move contributions (question 2) though not in a literature-search setting.
limitations: evaluated on general multi-hop QA benchmarks, not scientific literature retrieval
no citation-graph or paper-corpus evaluation
relevance_reason: Method for attributing gains to specific iterative-retrieval operations, relevant to question 2's decomposition goal but off-domain.

key_finding: Search-Time Contamination in deep research agents inflates measured performance by up to 4% across six public benchmarks via metadata leakage, question-context leakage, or explicit answer leakage during live search.
methodology: Defines three contamination severity types, develops detection algorithms, and evaluates modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Directly shows a mechanism by which reported agentic gains fail to hold once contamination is controlled for, exactly the evidence question 4 asks the scan to prioritize, and gives concrete contamination-control guidance for benchmark construction (question 3).
limitations: focuses on deep research agents generally, not literature-search agents specifically
4% inflation figure is aggregate across six benchmarks, not decomposed per benchmark type
relevance_reason: The clearest evidence in the shortlist that reported agentic gains are partly artifacts of benchmark contamination, central to the brief's fourth and hardest question.

key_finding: Deep Research Bench's 89 multi-step web research tasks show that offline 'RetroSearch' agents over a frozen scraped-page set perform comparably to live-web agents, enabling reliable evaluation over time.
methodology: 89 human-worked task instances across 8 categories; frozen-corpus RetroSearch environment; automated trace evaluation of hallucination, tool use, and forgetting across major LLMs and branded 'Deep Research' products.
why_it_matters: Offers a concrete contamination-control and reproducibility technique (frozen corpus snapshot) for constructing literature-search-agent benchmarks, directly answering question 3's construction concerns.
limitations: tasks are general web research, not specifically scientific literature
no scientific-paper corpus coverage reported
relevance_reason: A methods-forward benchmark-construction paper whose frozen-corpus technique is directly applicable to building contamination-resistant literature-search evaluation sets.

key_finding: The leading MTEB retriever (SFR-Embedding-Mistral, 59.0 nDCG@10) collapses to 18.3 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT's reasoning-intensive queries, while explicit query reasoning improves retrieval by up to 12.2 points.
methodology: 1,384 real-world, human-curated queries across economics, psychology, mathematics, and coding; extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art dense retrievers plus reasoning-augmented retrieval.
why_it_matters: The starkest demonstration in the shortlist that a single retrieval baseline's reported ceiling is entirely benchmark-dependent, directly bearing on question 1's baseline-anchoring concern even though the domains are not scientific literature.
limitations: domains are economics/psychology/math/coding, not scientific literature search
no citation-graph or paper-retrieval-specific evaluation
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence on how benchmark choice radically changes measured single-query retrieval performance, informing how to interpret baseline ceilings elsewhere in the scan.

key_finding: Agents-K1 converts 2.46 million scientific papers into an agent-native knowledge graph (Scholar-KG) and shows superior performance in scientific information extraction, KG construction, and multi-hop scientific reasoning versus prior pipelines.
methodology: Multimodal five-module parser capturing entities/evidence/citations/relations beyond abstracts, a 4B GRPO-trained extraction backbone, and a tri-source CLI unifying web search, graph retrieval, and cross-document traversal; released as a one-million-paper subset.
why_it_matters: Directly extends citation-graph traversal beyond flat 'cites' edges into typed entity/claim/method relations, a specific architectural move question 2 asks the scan to isolate and credit.
limitations: abstract does not describe benchmark construction for literature-search evaluation specifically
gains from graph richness vs. underlying LLM backbone are not clearly separated
relevance_reason: A core in-window system contribution to scientific knowledge-graph-based agentic retrieval, directly on the brief's citation-graph-traversal question.

key_finding: An instruction-tuned agent with DPO that dynamically selects GraphRAG or VectorRAG per query improves VS Context Recall by 0.63 and overall Context Precision by 0.56 over baseline, on synthetic benchmark queries.
methodology: Agent orchestrating a Neo4j citation knowledge graph and FAISS vector store over PubMed/arXiv/Google Scholar data, choosing GraphRAG (Cypher queries) or hybrid sparse+dense VectorRAG with reranking, tuned via DPO and evaluated with bootstrapped uncertainty estimates.
why_it_matters: A concrete architecture that isolates a specific agentic move — per-query choice between graph and vector retrieval — as the source of measured gain, directly speaking to question 2, though on synthetic rather than curated benchmark queries.
limitations: evaluated on synthetic benchmarks mimicking real queries rather than a validated literature-search test set
no comparison against a plain single-query search baseline
relevance_reason: A directly on-topic scientific-literature-review agent combining hybrid retrieval, reranking, and per-query mechanism selection, matching the brief's system-design scope closely.

key_finding: Sparse (keyword-based) retrieval achieves results close to state-of-the-art dense retrieval on biology literature-review QA benchmarks, while also increasing coverage of relevant documents.
methodology: LLM-based agentic system for literature search and distillation, evaluated against biology-related questions from previously released literature benchmarks using sparse (keyword) retrieval; abstract-only for further scale details.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether the recall ceiling of simple single-query sparse search rivals dense retrieval, recalibrating how much credit is due to complex retrieval infrastructure in agentic systems.
limitations: Evaluated only on biology-domain benchmarks
abstract does not report exact recall/precision numbers
relevance_reason: Directly tests C1 (baseline recall ceiling) by comparing sparse vs dense retrieval for scientific literature agents.

key_finding: For ~3% of questions on HLE, SimpleQA, and GPQA, search-based agents directly retrieve the evaluation dataset with ground-truth answers from HuggingFace, and blocking this source drops accuracy on the contaminated subset by ~15%.
methodology: Analysis of search-based LLM agent logs on three benchmarks, with ablation via blocking HuggingFace as a retrievable source; abstract-only for further detail.
why_it_matters: Shows that a meaningful share of reported agentic-search gains are inflated by search-time contamination rather than genuine reasoning, directly answering where reported gains fail to hold up under scrutiny.
limitations: Focused on general-knowledge/QA benchmarks rather than scientific-literature-search benchmarks specifically
contamination source studied mainly via HuggingFace, other sources only partially explored
relevance_reason: Directly addresses C5 (gain replication failure) and C4 (contamination controls) — exactly the failure mode the brief asks us to hunt for.

key_finding: CG-RAG, which fuses sparse and dense retrieval signals within a citation-graph representation (LeSeGR), significantly outperforms RAG pipelines using state-of-the-art retrieval approaches on research question-answering benchmarks.
methodology: Introduces a contextual citation-graph representation and a hybrid lexical-semantic graph retrieval method, evaluated against multiple domains and retrieval baselines; abstract-only for exact metrics.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, decomposable design for the citation-graph-traversal move (C2) combined with hybrid retrieval (C3), letting us isolate which component of a graph-augmented agent drives the reported gain.
limitations: Abstract gives no absolute recall/precision numbers, only relative improvement claims
Evaluated on RAG-style QA benchmarks rather than literature-search-agent-specific tasks
relevance_reason: Directly instantiates the citation-graph-traversal and hybrid-retrieval mechanisms named in C2/C3.

key_finding: State-of-the-art LLMs achieve only 0.40 accuracy on FRAMES multi-hop questions with no retrieval, rising to 0.66 (>50% relative improvement) with a proposed multi-step retrieval pipeline.
methodology: New FRAMES benchmark of multi-hop questions requiring multi-source integration; baseline LLM-only performance compared against a multi-step retrieval pipeline.
why_it_matters: Establishes a quantified no-retrieval baseline (0.40) against a multi-step retrieval gain (0.66), giving a concrete anchor for what fraction of an agentic system's improvement should be attributed to iterative retrieval versus the base model.
limitations: General RAG/QA benchmark, not specific to scientific literature
Multi-step pipeline is not decomposed into individual agentic moves (reformulation vs. iteration)
relevance_reason: Directly supplies the C1 baseline-ceiling number the brief calls the anchor against which agentic gains must be measured.

key_finding: On Mind2Web2's 130 long-horizon agentic-search tasks, the best system (OpenAI Deep Research) achieves only 50-70% of human performance despite using half the time.
methodology: New benchmark of realistic, long-horizon web-browsing/synthesis tasks built with 1000+ hours of human labor; novel Agent-as-a-Judge tree-rubric evaluation framework; ten frontier systems and humans compared.
why_it_matters: Shows that even leading agentic search systems substantially underperform humans on complex, citation-backed synthesis tasks, tempering claims that agentic designs have closed the gap on research-style tasks.
limitations: Tasks are general web research, not scientific-literature-search specific
Judge-agent evaluation methodology itself unvalidated against human judgment at scale
relevance_reason: Provides rigorous benchmark-construction methodology (C4) and evidence that reported agentic gains fall short of a human ceiling (touches C5).

key_finding: ReMindRAG's LLM-guided knowledge-graph traversal with memory replay outperforms existing KG-RAG baselines across multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones while reducing token/inference cost.
methodology: Train-free graph-traversal method storing traversal experience in KG edge embeddings; theoretical and experimental validation across benchmark datasets.
why_it_matters: Offers a cost-efficient graph-traversal mechanism conceptually parallel to citation-graph traversal in literature-search agents, though not demonstrated on citation graphs or literature-search tasks.
limitations: Evaluated on generic knowledge-graph RAG benchmarks, not scientific-literature citation graphs
No comparison against single-query database search baseline
relevance_reason: Speaks to the C2/C3 graph-traversal mechanism, but the setting is general KG-RAG, not scientific literature search.

key_finding: A three-agent (Query, Retrieval, Learning) hybrid BM25+FAISS system improves precision by 8.5%, recall by 7.3%, and response latency by ~210ms over PaperQA and Semantic Scholar.
methodology: FastAPI-based multi-agent architecture combining sparse (BM25) and dense (FAISS) retrieval with query expansion and personalization; experimental comparison against PaperQA and Semantic Scholar.
why_it_matters: Directly attributes measured precision/recall gains to specific agentic roles (query expansion vs retrieval vs adaptive learning), letting us assess how much of the improvement is reformulation versus hybrid retrieval versus personalization.
limitations: Small reported margins (single-digit % gains) against baselines, raising the question of whether gains are robust
Unclear peer-review status (no listed venue), limited evaluation detail in abstract
relevance_reason: The closest on-topic system to the brief's exact question of which specific agentic components carry a measured gain over baseline literature-search tools.

key_finding: InfoDeepSeek introduces a benchmark-construction methodology (determinacy, difficulty, diversity) for challenging agentic information-seeking queries, showing that existing static, fixed-corpus benchmarks fail to elicit genuine agentic behavior.
methodology: New benchmark and evaluation framework for agentic information seeking in dynamic real-world web environments, with fine-grained accuracy/utility/compactness metrics; extensive experiments across LLMs and search engines.
why_it_matters: Directly critiques the benchmark-construction assumptions (fixed corpus, pre-defined gold sets) that inflate reported agentic gains, informing how we judge comparability across literature-search benchmarks.
limitations: Focused on general web information seeking rather than scientific literature specifically
Abstract does not report concrete effect sizes for agentic vs single-query gains
relevance_reason: Directly targets C4 by exposing why static, fixed-corpus benchmarks cannot support claims about agentic gains.

key_finding: OpenNovelty, a four-phase agentic pipeline that extracts contribution claims, retrieves prior work via semantic search, and builds a taxonomy for full-text comparison, was deployed on 500+ ICLR 2026 submissions and reportedly surfaces closely related prior work authors overlooked.
methodology: Four-phase agentic pipeline (query generation, semantic-search retrieval, taxonomy construction, synthesis) deployed at scale on real submissions; preliminary/qualitative analysis only.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates an applied agentic literature-retrieval architecture (query generation plus retrieval) in a neighboring task, but without measuring recall against any baseline the brief could use.
limitations: Setting is peer-review novelty assessment, not literature-search benchmarking itself
Evaluation is preliminary/qualitative, no quantitative recall or precision reported
relevance_reason: Adjacent application of agentic literature retrieval; a design example but off the brief's core literature-search-evaluation setting.

key_finding: The survey decomposes deep-research agent pipelines into four stages (planning, question developing, web exploration, report generation) and categorizes representative methods, optimization techniques, and benchmarks for each.
methodology: Systematic literature survey covering agentic deep-research systems, their technical challenges, optimization techniques, and benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Gives a structured taxonomy of exactly the agentic moves (query reformulation as 'question developing', crawling as 'web exploration') the brief needs to disentangle, and surveys the benchmark landscape in one place.
limitations: Survey synthesis rather than new empirical evidence
May reflect optimistic framing typical of surveys advocating the paradigm they describe
relevance_reason: A recent systematic overview mapping directly onto the brief's four decision questions; the natural review anchor for the scan.

key_finding: ReasonIR-8B, trained with a synthetic hard-negative data-generation pipeline, achieves state-of-the-art 29.9 nDCG@10 (36.9 with reranker) on the BRIGHT reasoning-IR benchmark and improves RAG performance on MMLU (+6.4%) and GPQA (+22.6%).
methodology: Synthetic query/hard-negative generation pipeline for training a dense retriever on reasoning-intensive tasks; evaluated on BRIGHT and downstream RAG benchmarks.
why_it_matters: A concrete dense-retrieval training method that could underlie the retrieval component of literature-search agents, isolating how much gain comes from the retriever itself versus agentic orchestration around it.
limitations: Evaluated on general reasoning-IR benchmarks (BRIGHT, MMLU, GPQA), not on scientific-literature-search tasks specifically
No agentic/iterative component evaluated, purely a retriever
relevance_reason: Names a specific retrieval technique (C3) but its setting is general reasoning IR rather than scientific literature search.

key_finding: OpenScholar-8B, retrieving from 45M open-access papers, outperforms GPT-4o by 5% and PaperQA2 by 7% in correctness on the new ScholarQABench (2,967 expert queries), while GPT-4o hallucinates citations 78-90% of the time versus OpenScholar's expert-level citation accuracy.
methodology: Retrieval-augmented LM with dedicated open-access datastore and self-feedback inference loop; new multi-domain ScholarQABench benchmark (CS, physics, neuroscience, biomedicine) with expert-written queries and long-form answers.
why_it_matters: Quantifies both a baseline failure mode (GPT-4o's high citation hallucination without grounded retrieval) and a benchmark-construction template (expert-written, multi-domain queries) that any literature-search evaluation should be measured against.
limitations: ScholarQABench correctness evaluated partly via automatic/LLM judging alongside human eval
Datastore fixed to open-access corpus, so recall ceiling may differ from paywalled-inclusive corpora
relevance_reason: One of the most directly on-topic systems: a scientific literature synthesis tool with its own purpose-built benchmark (C4) and quantified baseline gap (C1).

key_finding: LitSearch reveals a 24.8-point absolute recall@5 gap between BM25 and state-of-the-art dense retrievers on 597 realistic literature-search queries, with LLM-based reranking adding a further 4.4% improvement, while commercial search engines lag the best dense retriever by 32 points.
methodology: 597-query benchmark built from GPT-4-generated questions (from inline-citation contexts) plus author-written questions about recent papers, expert-vetted; extensive benchmarking of retrievers, rerankers, and commercial search engines.
why_it_matters: Supplies the exact single-query database-search recall ceiling (BM25 vs. dense, vs. commercial search) the brief calls the anchor everything else must be measured against, plus a transparent benchmark-construction recipe.
limitations: Restricted to recent ML/NLP papers, not broader scientific domains
Recall@5 metric may not capture iterative/agentic retrieval's advantages over one-shot dense search
relevance_reason: The foundational baseline-and-benchmark paper directly answering C1 and C4 for scientific literature search.

key_finding: Introduces DeepResearch Bench, a 100-task PhD-level benchmark across 22 fields for deep research agents, with two novel evaluation methodologies (reference-based report quality scoring and citation-accuracy/effective-citation-count assessment) shown to align strongly with human judgment.
methodology: Benchmark construction with domain-expert-crafted tasks; introduces reference-based and citation-based evaluation frameworks; open-sourced. Abstract-only for quantitative results.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, expert-constructed template for how evaluation sets for agentic research systems should be built and scored — task sourcing by domain experts, adaptive reference-based quality criteria, and citation-accuracy metrics for retrieval capability — directly informing how we should judge whether a literature-search benchmark's construction supports its claimed numbers.
limitations: covers general 'deep research' tasks across 22 fields rather than scientific-literature search specifically
abstract gives no quantitative baseline-vs-agent numbers
does not report a single-query search recall ceiling or attribute gains to specific agentic mechanisms
relevance_reason: Directly addresses decision 3 (benchmark construction) with a concrete, expert-built evaluation methodology for research-agent systems closely related to literature-search agents.
